title: First mathematical model of a neural network
paper: "A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity", Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics
what_it_broke: Proved that networks of simple binary neurons can compute any logical function — the founding result of neural computation. Thought before: brains were beyond mathematics.
why_impossible: Nobody believed thought could be reduced to arithmetic on switches. This paper said it could, in 5 pages.

title: Turing Test — 'Can machines think?' gets an operational answer
paper: "Computing Machinery and Intelligence", Mind
what_it_broke: Replaced the unanswerable question 'can machines think?' with a measurable imitation game. Founded machine intelligence as an empirical discipline and predicted machine learning from scratch.
why_impossible: In 1950 computers had kilobytes of memory; proposing they could imitate human conversation was considered science fiction by working engineers.

title: Dartmouth Workshop — 'Artificial Intelligence' is named and founded as a field
paper: Dartmouth Summer Research Project proposal (1955)
what_it_broke: Coined the term 'artificial intelligence' and set the research agenda for the next 60 years: language, neural nets, self-improvement, abstraction.
why_impossible: The proposal claimed 'every aspect of learning or intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can simulate it' — a wildly bold claim for 1955 hardware.

title: Perceptron — first learning machine that trains itself
paper: "The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain", Psychological Review
what_it_broke: First algorithm where a machine adjusts its own weights from labeled examples instead of being programmed. Hardware Mark I perceptron learned to recognize images.
why_impossible: The New York Times reported it would soon 'walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence.' The hype outran a single-layer limit nobody had noticed yet.

title: First deep multilayer network trained by gradient descent (GMDH)
paper: "Cybernetic Predicting Devices"
what_it_broke: The first working deep-learning method: layer-by-layer training of arbitrarily deep networks, 40+ years before 'deep learning' was cool. Often called the deepest buried milestone in AI.
why_impossible: Published behind the Iron Curtain, ignored for decades, and everyone later rediscovered it from scratch believing depth was impossible to train.

title: ELIZA — first chatbot; users confide in a pattern matcher
paper: "ELIZA — A Computer Program For the Study of Natural Language Communication Between Man And Machine", CACM
what_it_broke: First program to hold a conversation good enough that humans poured their hearts out to it — the 'ELIZA effect' of over-attributing understanding is still named after this.
why_impossible: Weizenbaum was horrified: his secretary asked him to leave the room so she could chat privately with ~200 lines of keyword matching.

title: Backpropagation through arbitrary networks envisioned (Linnainmaa)
paper: "The representation of the cumulative rounding error of an algorithm as a Taylor expansion of the local rounding errors", Master's thesis
what_it_broke: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation — the exact mechanism inside every deep net trained today — invented as numerical analysis, not AI.
why_impossible: It sat unused for ML for 16 years because nobody had networks worth differentiating.

title: Backpropagation popularized — multilayer nets finally trainable
paper: "Learning representations by back-propagating errors", Nature
what_it_broke: Showed hidden layers learn internal representations, breaking Minsky & Papert's single-layer dead end and reviving neural networks after a 15-year freeze.
why_impossible: The 1969 'Perceptrons' book had convinced most of the field that multilayer training was a lost cause.

title: Convolutional neural networks — weight sharing inspired by visual cortex
paper: "Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition", Neural Computation
what_it_broke: LeNet read real US zip codes and checks. Convolutions made vision tractable and became the substrate of all modern computer vision.
why_impossible: Training on actual handwritten mail data with 1989 compute meant backprop through convolutions at scale was widely thought impractical.

title: TD-Gammon — reinforcement learning reaches world-class play with zero human coaching
paper: "Temporal difference learning and TD-Gammon", CACM
what_it_broke: Learned backgammon purely by playing itself, reaching top-human level and inventing moves humans then adopted. First proof that RL + neural nets can exceed human strategy without imitation.
why_impossible: The idea that superhuman skill could emerge from pure self-play with no expert knowledge contradicted the entire symbolic-AI playbook of the era.

title: Deep Blue defeats Kasparov — chess falls to machines
paper: "Deep Blue", Artificial Intelligence journal (2002 retrospective)
what_it_broke: World chess champion beaten in a formal match — the first time a reigning human champion of an intellectual sport fell to a machine.
why_impossible: Kasparov had said no computer would beat a grandmaster 'in his lifetime.' It happened 6 years later.

title: LSTM — memory cells solve vanishing gradients over time
paper: "Long Short-Term Memory", Neural Computation
what_it_broke: Made sequence learning actually work — RNNs that remember across hundreds of steps. LSTM ran speech recognition, translation, and handwriting systems for a decade before Transformers replaced it.
why_impossible: Vanishing gradients were considered a fundamental wall for recurrent nets since 1991; LSTM tunneled under it with gated memory cells.

title: Deep Belief Networks — 'deep learning' rebranded and made trainable
paper: "A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets", Neural Computation
what_it_broke: Layer-wise unsupervised pretraining showed deep architectures could be trained effectively, directly triggering the modern deep learning era and its name.
why_impossible: For 20 years reviewers rejected any deep-net paper as 'obviously doomed by local minima'; this broke the taboo.

title: ImageNet — the dataset bet that scaled vision
paper: "ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database", CVPR
what_it_broke: 14 million labeled images turned progress into a measurable race. The insight that DATA, not architecture, was the bottleneck set up everything after 2012.
why_impossible: Colleagues told Fei-Fei Li a grad student couldn't label enough images in a lifetime; she used Amazon Mechanical Turk crowdsourcing instead.

title: AlexNet — GPUs crush ImageNet, error drops 10 points overnight
paper: "ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks", NeurIPS
what_it_broke: Top-5 error fell from 26% to 15.3% — the largest single-year jump in vision history. The entire field pivoted to deep learning within months; GPU-compute scaling became the roadmap.
why_impossible: Classical vision researchers expected incremental gains forever. One student project on two gaming GPUs ended classical feature engineering as a discipline.

title: Word2Vec — meaning becomes geometry; king − man + woman = queen
paper: "Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality", NeurIPS
what_it_broke: Showed word meaning emerges as linear structure in embedding space from raw text co-occurrence alone — semantics you can do arithmetic on, with no labels.
why_impossible: Semantic relationships with algebraic regularity emerging from plain statistics felt like magic; many assumed such structure required hand-built knowledge graphs.

title: DQN learns Atari from pixels — one network, 49 games, no game-specific code
paper: "Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning", arXiv / Nature 2015
what_it_broke: One architecture mastered games from raw screen pixels with only score feedback — general intelligence behavior in miniature, and the moment DeepMind's AGI thesis became credible.
why_impossible: RL was thought hopelessly unstable when combined with deep nets; experience replay + target networks tamed it, stunning both fields.

title: GANs — two networks duel and photorealistic generation begins
paper: "Generative Adversarial Networks", NeurIPS
what_it_broke: Introduced adversarial training: a forger vs detective game producing images indistinguishable from photos within years. Opened the generative-media era.
why_impossible: Reportedly sketched in a single night; making two competing networks converge instead of collapse was considered hopeless instability.

title: AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol — Go falls a decade early; Move 37
paper: "Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search", Nature
what_it_broke: Beat the world's best at Go, which experts said was 10+ years away. Move 37 of game 2 was a move no human would play — and won the game. Creativity without instruction.
why_impossible: Go's search space dwarfed chess by orders of magnitude; experts estimated decades remaining. It took 18 months from DQN.

title: Attention Is All You Need — the Transformer
paper: "Attention Is All You Need", NeurIPS
what_it_broke: Removed recurrence entirely; pure attention parallelizes across sequences. Became the architecture underneath GPT, BERT, Claude, Gemini, image/video diffusion, and protein models — possibly the most consequential ML architecture ever.
why_impossible: Recurrence was assumed essential for language; deleting it and winning translation benchmarks within a year was heresy that worked.

title: BERT — pretrain once, fine-tune everywhere
paper: "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding", NAACL
what_it_broke: Established the pretrain → fine-tune paradigm; one model beat state-of-the-art on 11 NLP benchmarks. Made transfer learning the default recipe for all of NLP.
why_impossible: NLP was a zoo of task-specific engineering; the claim that ONE pretrained model could dominate every task simultaneously upended the field's methodology.

title: GPT-1 — generative pretraining hints that scale predicts ability
paper: "Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training"
what_it_broke: Showed plain next-word prediction on raw internet text produces transferable understanding. Planted the scaling hypothesis that became OpenAI's whole strategy.
why_impossible: Language modeling was dismissed as a toy objective; betting the company on 'predict the next word well enough and understanding emerges' looked insane.

title: GPT-3 — 175B parameters; few-shot learning emerges from scale
paper: "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners", NeurIPS
what_it_broke: Without fine-tuning, GPT-3 performed tasks from natural-language instructions alone. In-context learning appeared at scale like a phase transition — nobody had engineered it.
why_impossible: The field consensus was bigger models would be marginally better at grammar. Instead new CAPABILITIES emerged that smaller versions lacked entirely.

title: Scaling Laws — capability follows power laws predictably
paper: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models", arXiv
what_it_broke: Turned model-building into engineering: loss decreases as a smooth predictable power law across 8 orders of magnitude. Companies could now forecast billion-dollar training runs before spending them.
why_impossible: ML had always been alchemy — tune and pray. Discovering that performance was FORECASTABLE changed AI from craft to industry and justified massive capital bets.

title: Copilot — LLMs write production code
paper: "Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code", arXiv
what_it_broke: First mass-market tool where an AI writes functional software inside developers' editors. Programming became the first profession transformed in daily practice.
why_impossible: Code generation was thought to need formal verification and syntax-aware design; a text predictor outperformed dedicated program synthesis systems.

title: CLIP + DALL·E — text-to-image and zero-shot vision
paper: "Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP)"; "Zero-Shot Text-to-Image Generation (DALL·E)"
what_it_broke: CLIP matched ResNet-50 on ImageNet with ZERO training examples via web text supervision; DALL·E generated coherent images from sentences. Modalities fused into one representational space.
why_impossible: Cross-modal grounding was a decade-old dream requiring curated labels; raw web-scale pairs did it better than anyone predicted.

title: Stable Diffusion — photorealistic generation goes open-weight
paper: "High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models", CVPR
what_it_broke: Latent diffusion cut generation compute by orders of magnitude AND shipped open weights — anyone could run frontier-quality image generation on a gaming PC, unleashing an ecosystem.
why_impossible: Frontier labs assumed generative quality required datacenter budgets; suddenly it ran locally, and the closed-source moat evaporated for images.

title: ChatGPT — AI reaches 100M users; the public era begins
paper: "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT)", PNAS
what_it_broke: RLHF-aligned chat crossed from research demo to fastest-adopted consumer product in history (~100M users in 2 months). AI stopped being a field and became infrastructure overnight.
why_impossible: It was a low-key research-preview release of technology labs already had; NOBODY — including OpenAI — predicted the societal detonation. The surprise was cultural, not technical.

title: AlphaFold2 releases 200M protein structures — a 50-year grand challenge solved
paper: "Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold", Nature
what_it_broke: Solved protein folding prediction at experimental accuracy and gave away ALL structures — 200 million of them, nearly every known protein. Structural biology compressed decades into a database query.
why_impossible: Levinthal's paradox implied folding prediction was computationally hopeless; CASP13 in 2018 still had mediocre results. Two years later the 50-year problem was DONE, and Nobel-level impact followed in 2024.

title: GPT-4 — multimodal reasoning; passes professional exams
paper: "GPT-4 Technical Report", arXiv
what_it_broke: Passed the bar exam at ~90th percentile, aced medical licensing exams, handled images. First model widely argued to show 'sparks of AGI' in Microsoft Research's famous analysis.
why_impossible: Professional licensure was THE human expertise moat; a next-token predictor clearing it forced society-wide reassessment of what 'knowledge work' means.

title: LLaMA leak — near-frontier weights escape into everyone's hands
paper: "LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models", arXiv
what_it_broke: Research-only weights leaked within a week; fine-tunes (Alpaca, Vicuna) proved frontier-adjacent capability ran on laptops. The open-weights ecosystem exploded permanently.
why_impossible: Closed labs' core assumption — capability advantage requires control of weights — was publicly falsified when a leaked 7B fine-tune rivaled early ChatGPT on many tasks.

title: Tool use & plugins — LLMs act on the world; AutoGPT moment
paper: "Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools" (Meta, precursor)
what_it_broke: Models began calling APIs, browsing, executing code, chaining goals autonomously. AutoGPT hit #1 on GitHub faster than any repo before it. The agent era started here.
why_impossible: LLMs were conversational mirrors; giving them hands and letting them plan multi-step actions unprompted was a category jump nobody shipped deliberately at scale before.

title: Sora — minute-long coherent video from text; world-simulator claims
paper: "Video generation models as world simulators" (technical report)
what_it_broke: Minute-long, physically-plausible multi-shot video emerged from diffusion transformers at scale. Object permanence and 3D consistency appeared WITHOUT explicit physics programming.
why_impossible: Video coherence past seconds was considered blocked by compounding errors; emergent object permanence suggested video models learn implicit world models — a philosophical earthquake.

title: o1 — inference-time 'thinking' becomes a new scaling axis
paper: "Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Without Prompting" / o1 system card; "Let's Verify Step by Step" (process supervision)
what_it_broke: Spending more COMPUTE AT INFERENCE made models dramatically smarter — IMO gold-medal math, PhD-level science. A second scaling dimension beyond parameters/training was opened.
why_impossible: Scaling laws were about TRAINING compute; discovering test-time compute scaled too doubled the road ahead and reset every capability ceiling estimate.

title: Nobel Prizes go to neural network pioneers — twice in one week
paper: Physics: Hopfield networks & Boltzmann machines; Chemistry: AlphaFold2 & protein design
what_it_broke: Physics Nobel to Hinton+Hopfield, Chemistry Nobel to Hassabis+Jumper+Baker — the establishment canonization of AI as foundational science, 42 years after the field was laughed at.
why_impossible: Neural networks spent decades as a discredited fringe; two Nobels in one week for connectionism would have been unthinkable even five years prior.

title: DeepSeek-V3 — frontier-class training for ~$5.6M
paper: "DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report", arXiv
what_it_broke: 671B-parameter MoE trained on ~2048 GPUs for a fraction of Western costs via FP8 precision + Multi-head Latent Attention + load-balancing innovations. Cost-of-frontier collapsed.
why_impossible: Everyone assumed frontier training required $500M+ runs on 100k+ GPU clusters; export controls were supposed to keep China behind. Both assumptions broke at once.

title: DeepSeek-R1 — open-weights reasoning model matches o1; markets panic
paper: "DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning", arXiv
what_it_broke: Pure RL produced verifiable reasoning chains matching OpenAI's closed o1 — released OPEN WEIGHTS, MIT license. Nvidia lost ~$600B market cap in one day, the largest single-stock loss in history. App #1 worldwide.
why_impossible: Three assumptions died together: (1) reasoning needs closed frontier labs, (2) RL-for-reasoning needs secret recipes, (3) export controls guarantee Western lead. A Chinese hedge-fund lab shattered all three for ~$5M.

title: Agentic coding goes mainstream — Claude Code, Devin, OpenHands
paper: "SWE-bench Verified: Proving autonomous software engineering" (evaluation lineage)
what_it_broke: Agents completing real multi-hour engineering tasks — resolving GitHub issues end-to-end — moved from demo to daily tool. SWE-bench Verified pass rates climbed from 4% to >70% within a year.
why_impossible: Long-horizon autonomy was supposed to be years away due to compounding errors; agentic scaffolding + better models got there while skeptics were writing explainers about why it couldn't work.
